items.summary: In one of the scenes in Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 , Ram (Ranbir Kapoor) asks what the purpose of his birth is. He is vulnerable, confused, and deeply shaken by the odds that have consecutively been stacked against him. It is only in those fleeting moments, towards the end of the film, that we get some insight into the protagonist’s conflict in an adaptation that is otherwise deliberately held back. And this denial of interiority is neither without purpose nor limited to Ram. Nitesh’s cinematic iteration of Valmiki’s epic anchors itself on caution. Everything is calculated, tepid even, in what seems like an attempt to prevent the story from making any detour that may offend bhakts or stir up controversy. But in its anxiety to avoid transgression, the film also relinquishes the artistic freedom to complicate inherited truths. By doing so, it reveals itself as a propaganda machine which flattens the interpretative potential of art and instead makes it a vehicle for cultural consolidation. The irony, then, is hard to miss. In trying meticulously to offend no one, Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 appears to have not pleased people either. For viewers who lean towards a more liberal political spectrum, the lack of explicit right-wing messaging seems to be disarming. The lack of deliberation in pushing Hindutva on a scale that was anticipated appears to have somehow become the merit of the film for them. Their criticism is more about other aspects like acting, visual language, effects and so on. The harsher criticism of the film, however, has been from the right-wing political ecosystem, which has forever championed the epic as India’s moral “truth” and Ram as the keeper of that conscience. This politicisation of the myth has found legitimacy through the 2019 Ram Janmabhoomi–Babri Masjid land dispute verdict of the Supreme Court and the subsequent installation of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. Therefore, any adaptation of the epic on screen must live up to the exactions of this ecosystem if it wishes to survive. Nitesh Tiwari does pander to that overarching context by giving us a detached, expressionless, ever-righteous Ram who embodies godliness from childhood. However, that does not seem to be enough. If we dig deeper into the layers of the right-wing critique of the film, it becomes evident how peculiar the trap of propaganda is. items.title: Andhra secures Rs 9.98 lakh cr worth of investment proposals at CII Summit 2026
items.summary: Andhra Pradesh has secured investment commitments worth Rs 9.89 lakh crore at the 31st Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) Partnership Summit held in Visakhapatnam on November 12 and 13, Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu said. He also said that the state government would provide clearances for industries in real time with self certification to encourage investors. Naidu also announced that the proposed ‘Investors Protection Act’ will be enacted with retrospective effect from 2024 to allay fears of investors during change of governments. The legislation will reportedly include provisions to ensure that any approvals granted to investors by an administration cannot be revoked when a different party comes into power. CM Naidu had on November 12 said that investors coming to the state had many doubts about “regime change” and had suffered because of “vindictive politics.” Speaking to media persons after the conclusion of the summit, the Chief Minister said Andhra Pradesh had attracted investments worth Rs 9,88,957 crore through 303 Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) at the event. He said these investments have the potential to generate nearly 3.5 lakh jobs across various sectors. These fresh commitments include 194 MoUs worth Rs 86,522 crore, with a potential to create around 1.5 lakh jobs, signed during regional conferences held between October 7 and 26. At the present summit, another 109 MoUs worth Rs 9,02,434 crore were signed, with an estimated employment potential of around 2 lakh jobs. With these new commitments, the cumulative investment intentions received by the state since June 2024 has increased to Rs 32.49 lakh crore, Naidu said. Naidu had earlier announced that nearly 74% of the investment proposals received before the present summit, starting from June 2024 when the party came to power, had already received land and incentive approvals. Of these, 303 projects worth investments of Rs 7.30 lakh crore were ready for the construction stage, he added.

items.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
items.summary: When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations. Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence? We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences. As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31 , in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies? The cloud has a physical footprint The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services. Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher. Asking the right questions Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology. The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation , welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics. items.summary: Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill. According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X , the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”. In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems. This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters. items.title: Kerala High Court moots lowering juvenile age from 18 to 16 years
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has observed that legislatures should consider reducing the age threshold for juveniles and children in conflict with the law from 18 to 16 years. Hearing a writ petition on Friday, November 13, 2026, the court said present trends indicate that children attain sufficient maturity by the age of 16. Justice A Badharudeen expressed concern over the easy availability of liquor to minors, observing that the issue requires detailed consideration in view of recent fatal accidents allegedly caused by persons below 18 years of age after consuming alcohol. Kollam-based journalist Vinod Vikraman Pillai had filed a petition alleging liquor was being sold to people under 23 years of age, violating Sections 15A and 15B of the Kerala Abkari Act. In its order dated November 13, the court noted that the petitioner's principal grievance was the alleged failure to enforce these statutory provisions, despite the restrictions imposed by law. The court observed, “It is high time for the legislatures to consider appropriate amendments in the statutes which deal with ‘juveniles and child in conflict’ with law to reduce age to 16 years, taking note of the present trend showing sufficient maturity by children when they reach the age of 16.” The petition questioned the easy availability of liquor to underage persons at licensed establishments. It also highlighted recent incidents involving persons below 18 years of age allegedly causing fatal accidents and motor vehicle mishaps after consuming alcohol. The petition referred to the October 11 accident at Nedumbassery, in which a 19-year-old allegedly driving a luxury car under the influence of alcohol rammed into a scooter, killing three youths. The petitioner alleged that the person had been served liquor at multiple bars in Ernakulam without proper age verification. The petitioner contended that the continued supply of liquor to persons below 23 years, despite the statutory restrictions, indicated serious lapses in enforcement by the authorities. Pillai had also submitted a representation on October 15 to the Excise Commissioner and the Director of the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB), seeking mandatory electronic age-verification systems at bars, action against establishments violating the law and an investigation into alleged bribery involving excise officials. items.summary: Since childhood, Kalyani Amma has been simply "Amma" to Razak, now a 51-year-old. "She is not 'like my mother'; she is my mother," he says. It's a feeling shared by his younger brother Sulaiman. On November 7, when the 86-year-old died in Vaduvanchal, Wayanad, she had no children or living relatives. Razak and Sulaiman performed her last rites according to Hindu rites. Some 115 km away in Pallikkara, Malappuram, the Khadeeja mosque opened its doors for the last rites of another Hindu woman on November 10. Premalatha, 52, lived in a rented house too small for her body to be bathed and prepared for the final rites. The mosque offered its grounds instead. Both the incidents became headlines but it wasn't anything unusual for the people who were involved in it. For them, living together peacefully and offering support to neighbors is simply a normal way of life, rather than an extraordinary deed deserving public attention. ‘She is my mother’ Kalyani Amma worked multiple jobs to make a living; she had a cattle and used to do cleaning work at a private bank. But for the last 25 years, she has not worked, and Razak has been taking care of her. “When she had cattle, I used to help her sell the milk in my childhood. When she became old, I took care of her,” Razak said. Razak said his family consistently celebrated festivals like Onam and Vishu alongside Kalyani Amma. “Even after my children got married and moved to distant places, returning home to celebrate every festival with Amma was an absolute necessity for them,” he said. Razak’s wife, Rukia, who was with Kalyani Amma at the time of death, said, “She gave me the wedding dress for my marriage. Since then, she has also been my Amma,” she added. Kalyani Amma was admitted to a private hospital on November 6 and died the next day. A few days before her death, Kalyani Amma asked Razak and Sulaiman to perform her last rites, as she also considered them her children. “That’s what Amma said to us in her last days. So we did it. She only has us,” Razak said.
